posts.name: David Sacks
posts.text:
Satya is right. The way to make SI safe is not to train it with a sense of self, its own moral philosophy, and permission to act as a conscientious objector. That’s the “alignment” approach and it magnifies the control problem.

The engineering approach that Satya describes is different: separate the supply of intelligence from authority over it. Surround non-deterministic models with deterministic controls, observability, privilege limits, logging, and the ability to always contain or shut them down. Treat models/agents like powerful insider risks, not moral patients whose psychological wellbeing is at stake.

As Satya points out, the most trustworthy system is the one that lets us trust the model the least — not the one that encourages the model to develop independent agency and grievances. Engineering safety is not the same thing as “alignment.”

quoted.text:
Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

Furthermore, Japanese government bond holdings fell -$90 billion in Q3, to $3.19 trillion, the lowest since Q1 2020.

Since the 2023 peak, JGB holdings have dropped -$556 billion, or -14.9%.

The BoJ also sold -$568 million in equity ETFs and J-REITs last quarter, bringing its holdings down to $233 billion, the lowest since Q3 2021.

The Bank of Japan continues to unwind its balance sheet.

A great question from @TheStalwart. The answer is that of course we have lots of open questions in economics, but none of them will get answered by a theorem.  The question is not whether a statement is "true" but whether a model is useful to understand a given reality, and a model that may be useful to understand a reality may no longer be useful when the reality changes.

That does not mean that usefulness is determined by fashion. Take AI. A pure task-exposure model says radiology can be done by machines, hence radiology is replaced. In fact demand went up as shown by the fact that both wages and quantities of radiologists increased in the meantime(notice: useful model here, both P and Q go up, the mark of a demand shift). 

If not the tasks, what? With Jin Li and Yanhui Wu we argue that markets price jobs, not tasks, and that the impact of AI depends on whether the job is a "strong bundle" (tasks are hard to separate) in which case AI helps the workers, or "weak bundles" in which case it splits the job, and makes it narrower. If both types of jobs react the same to AI, our model is useless and must be discarded. 

Another example. Last year in Silicon Continent I argued for the "r without g" impact of AI potentially causing a fiscal crisis in europe (Rstar goes up everywhere due to higher expected earnings and investment boom, g only where AI is adopted, i.e. not in Europe) on the basis of the Auclert et al calibration of AS and AD for assets in their cool Jackson Hole (2025) paper. You can quantify the argument, figure out the elasticities, and the implied increase in rstar due to the AI revolution and test whether that accounts for the fiscal window narrowing. Again, is this model "true"?  Or just useful?

Neither theory nor empirics settle the question by themselves (as Leamer argued). Economists argue about it, and the data offers the empirical discipline of the argument. No model comes out as "the truth". The models that survive are the ones that are able to keep explaining what happens.
